**Differential of an Inverse Function.**

Consider the function (see p. 13) y = 3x; it can be expressed in the form $x=\frac{y}{3}$; this latter form is called the inverse function to the one originally given.

If $y=3x,\frac{dy}{dx}$ = 3; if $x=\frac{y}{3},\frac{dx}{dy}=\frac{1}{3}$, and we see that

$$
\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{1}{dx}
$$

or $\frac{dy}{dx}\times\frac{dx}{dy}=1.$ dy Consider $y=4x^{2},\frac{dy}{dx}=8x$; the inverse function is 1 1 $x=^{y}\frac{1_{2}}{2},$ and $\frac{dx}{dy}=&#95;{4}\sqrt{y}=&#95;{4\times2x}=\frac{1}{8x}.$

Here again

$$
\frac{dy}{dx}\times\frac{dx}{dy}=1.
$$

It can be shown that for all functions which can be put into the inverse form, one can always write $\frac{dy}{dx}\times\frac{dx}{dy}=1$ $\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{1}{dx}.$
